Judicial Branch Announces Procedure for Emergency Case Filings Regarding Elections

Date: 10/29/2026

AUGUSTA, Maine. The Maine Judicial Branch announced the procedure for emergency case filings regarding elections to be held on November 3, 2026.

Procedure for Election Filings

In order to expedite the review of filings, Superior Court Chief Justice Robert Mullen and District Court Chief Judge Brent Davis issued a standing order on October 28th requiring all filings pertaining to the November 3 election and filed between Friday, October 30, 2026, at 4:00 pm and Tuesday, November 3, 2026, at 9:00 pm to be filed on paper at the clerk's office. Filers should NOT use the eFile Maine system for these emergency filings.

Filings submitted on paper will be reviewed immediately by a clerk and can be directed to the appropriate justice for timely review. Filers are also encouraged to put their cell phone numbers or emergency telephone numbers (where they can be reached after hours) on their filings.

State Courts Open Late on November 3

The state courthouses in Bangor, Augusta and Portland will be open until 9:00 p.m. for the purpose of accepting and acting on emergency paper filings regarding elections. A judge, a clerk and a marshal will be on duty at each courthouse.

Availability of Documents to the Media

All public documents related to election filings will be posted on the high-profile page of the Judicial Branchs public website as soon as is practicable.

Judicial Branch Issues Amendment to Administrative Order on the Maine Rules of Electronic Court Systems (MRECS), Effective November 2, 2026

Date: 11/2/2026

The Maine Judicial Branch announced today that an Administrative Order on rules and procedures applicable to Maine eCourts and eFiling has been amended regarding the use of non-Judicial Branch court forms when one has been provided by the court.

AO JB 20-03 (A. 11-26) was adopted in 2020 to provide guidance on the applicability of the Maine Rules of Electronic Court Systems (MRECS) during the transitional period during the implementation of Maine eCourts and electronic filing when there are conflicts between MRECS and other Judicial Branch rules and administrative orders.

New Section I.C. of JB 20-20 provides that "[i]f an applicable court-approved form exists and is available to the public, the parties must use it" and further adds the following requirement:

"If a filer does not use a form, the filer must include a brief explanation in a cover letter accompanying the submission that indicates the existing form is not suitable."

Barbara Cardone, Director of Legal Affairs and Public Relations explained the reason for the amendment. "The reason for the amendment is to increase the efficiency of reviewing eFiling submissions. eFilers who submit non-Judicial Branch-approved court forms can avoid having their submission rejected by including an explanatory cover letter with the eFiling. We hope this clarification helps the eFiling and legal community's smooth transition to eFiling and Maine eCourts."

AO JB 20-03 (A. 11-26) has been posted on the Administrative Orders page of the Judicial Branch website at https://www.courts.maine.gov/adminorders/index.html

item.description: This final rule sets forth routine updates to the Medicare home health payment rates in accordance with existing statutory and regulatory requirements. In addition, this final rule discusses the behavior adjustments and finalizes a temporary behavior adjustment. It also finalizes the recalibrated case-mix weights and updated functional impairment levels; comorbidity subgroups; and low-utilization payment adjustment (LUPA) thresholds for CY 2027. Additionally, this final rule discusses and responds to comments on the provision of home health palliative care services and includes a summary of comments received on the request for information (RFI) on a home health specific wage index included in the proposed rule. item.description: The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA or Department) proposes to amend the regulations governing grazing and livestock use on the National Forest System to modernize grazing administration, improve clarity, codify existing policy, and expand opportunities for stewardship and access. The proposed amendments would update permit issuance, eligibility, and qualification provisions; establish a framework for adaptive response to drought, wildfire, and similar disturbance events; and expand authorities for stewardship-oriented livestock use, including adding the ability to implement stewardship projects (such as outcome-based grazing or targeted grazing) under a temporary grazing permit or livestock use permit. The proposed rule would revise grazing fee provisions to ensure consistent fee-setting across the national forests in the 16 contiguous Western States and the national grasslands, and establish a surcharge for authorized leasing of livestock by permittees. It would consolidate and renumber existing sections in subpart A for clarity and make conforming, technical, and administrative updates throughout part 222. The Department invites public comment on all aspects of the proposed rule.

The proposed rule modernizes the Permanent Labor Certification program by strengthening recruitment standards and recordkeeping requirements, eliminating administrative exemptions to the statutory labor market test, and improving safeguards for all American workers, especially those affected by layoffs. This proposed update to the PERM program – the first comprehensive set of regulatory reforms to the program in nearly 20 years – will ensure that highly qualified American workers receive fair consideration and first access to job opportunities.“American Workers are the best in the world, and they deserve the first and best job opportunities. Existing regulations have instead allowed companies to sponsor foreign workers without fully considering American workers first,” said Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling. “This proposed rule change will ensure American workers are first in line for high-skilled, high-paying job opportunities over foreign labor.”The proposed rule would require employers to level the playing field when recruiting workers by using the same channels and methods when advertising jobs. Proposed changes include a requirement to replace print-based job advertisements with online recruiting through employer websites, online job boards, social media, job fairs, and campus recruitment. Employers would also be required to advertise positions for at least 90 calendar days and demonstrate that they made good-faith efforts to recruit qualified American workers. Under the proposal, employers would be prohibited from tailoring job opportunities to foreign workers. The department also proposed to eliminate the administrative exemption employers used to bypass the statutory labor market test for certain occupations. Under the proposal, employers recruiting for physical therapists, nurses, and workers with exceptional abilities in the sciences or arts would be required to consider qualified U.S. workers. The proposed rule also protects qualified American workers affected by layoffs by requiring ongoing consideration of laid off workers throughout the labor certification and immigrant petition processes, and prohibiting certain employers that have laid off American workers within the last 2 years from seeking permanent labor certification for the same or similar positions. Comments on the proposed rule are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register. Additional information is available on ETA’s Office of Foreign Labor Certification website.

The policy change follows best practices for courthouse security and aligns with the policy of the federal courts in Maine and the state courts of most other New England states.

The Judicial Branch stopped issuing security cards to attorneys in May 2026. Attorneys whose security cards have not expired by January 1, 2027, will be able to receive a pro rata refund of the fee for the unexpired portion. item.content:encoded: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division today announced a final rule to revise its analysis for distinguishing between employees and independent contractors under the Fair Labor Standards Act and two related federal laws. The new final rule provides clarity to businesses and workers alike, as well as the division’s enforcement personnel.U.S. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling, Wage and Hour Division Administrator Andrew Rogers, and other department officials hosted an event to formally announce the final rule at the Frances Perkins Building this morning. Employers, business associations, worker advocates, independent contractors, and other stakeholders were in attendance as Secretary Sonderling highlighted the clarity and simplicity of the new regulations.The final rule rescinds an earlier 2024 rule addressing the classification of employees and independent contractors and replaces it with an analysis that is substantially similar to the framework adopted by the department in 2021. Consistent with the outcomes of federal appellate cases, the final rule provides further guidance on the process for differentiating between employees with protections under the FLSA and individuals who work as independent contractors.“It’s more important than ever to ensure our labor regulations keep pace with the changing ways that Americans choose to work, and businesses choose to operate,” said Secretary Sonderling. “The new Independent Contractor final rule establishes clear, predictable, and easy-to-understand criteria for determining who is an employee and who is an independent contractor – allowing millions of Americans to take advantage of new opportunities in President Trump’s booming economy.”The final rule also applies the department’s streamlined analysis to the Family and Medical Leave Act, and the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act, both of which use the FLSA’s statutory definition of “employ.” However, the rule does not change the assessment of employee or independent contractor status for the purpose of any other federal laws, including the Internal Revenue Code, and does not preempt any state or local laws.“The Department of Labor is committed to helping employers prevent misclassification. This rule strikes the right balance by protecting employees who are entitled to the protections of federal wage and hour laws, while also respecting the entrepreneurial spirit of legitimate independent contractors,” said Administrator Rogers. “The department distilled longstanding judicial tests into a framework that employees and employers can reliably apply at the outset of business relationships.”The analysis in the department’s final rule does the following:Applies an “economic reality” test to determine whether a worker is in business for himself or herself as an independent contractor or is an employee economically dependent on an employer for work.Identifies and explains two “core factors” to help determine if a worker is economically dependent on an employer for work or in business for himself or herself:The nature and degree of control over the work.The worker’s opportunity for profit or loss based on initiative and/or investment.Identifies other factors to help determine a worker’s status as an employee or independent contractor, including the amount of skill required for the work, the degree of permanence of the working relationship, and whether the work is part of an integrated unit of production.Advises that the actual practice of the worker and the potential employer is more relevant than what may be contractually or theoretically possible.Provides 14 fact-specific examples applying the factors to real-life circumstances. The department published a notice of proposed rulemaking on Feb. 27, 2026, and received approximately 16,500 public comments during a 60-day comment period. After reviewing this feedback, the department finalized the rule with modifications and enhancements. For example, in response to commenter requests, the final rule includes new illustrative examples involving farm labor contractors, digital platform workers, and truck drivers.Workers and employers can contact the Wage and Hour Division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). The agency’s PAID program offers employers an opportunity to self-report and resolve potential minimum wage and overtime violations under the FLSA, as well as certain potential violations under the FMLA.WATCH the Independent Contractor Final Rule Announcement.Read Secretary Sonderling’s Op-Ed on the Final Rule.Read the final rule, which takes effect 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

item.content:encoded: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor’s Employee Benefits Security Administration today issued proposed amendments to the investment duties regulation to clarify the fiduciary duty of loyalty under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act.The proposed rule seeks to end the 32-year uncertainty surrounding whether ERISA allows fiduciaries to consider non-financial factors in retirement plan investments, including environmental, social, and governance, and diversity, equity, and inclusion. The proposal gives fiduciaries an affirmative expression of their duty of loyalty, which would clarify that ERISA requires plan fiduciaries to act solely in the interest of the plan’s participants and beneficiaries, and for the exclusive purpose of providing for the interests of participants and beneficiaries in their retirement income or financial benefits under the plan.“President Trump’s Department of Labor is not putting its thumb on the scale for or against any particular investment or asset class,” said U.S. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling. “Our proposed rule makes clear that retirement plan fiduciaries must make investment decisions solely in the financial interests of workers and retirees, not to advance political or social agendas. Our focus is on protecting and growing Americans’ retirement savings, which have reached record levels thanks to President Trump.”If finalized, the proposal would also place a heightened focus on shareholder engagement and proxy voting by fiduciaries to secure the retirement interests of American workers and would avoid the improper pressures and influence placed on plan fiduciaries. This includes voting shares and otherwise attempting to influence corporate behavior through shareholder engagement activities for ESG/DEI purposes. The proposed rule follows the directive in President Trump’s executive order, “Protecting American Investors from Foreign-Owned and Politically Motivated Proxy Advisors,” which instructed the department to strengthen the fiduciary standards of pension and retirement plans covered by ERISA.“President Trump has directed the department to assess whether certain proxy advisor firms spreading ESG and DEI are acting solely in the financial interest of plan participants,” said Assistant Secretary for the Employee Benefits Security Administration Daniel Aronowitz. “Our proposed rule does just that by making clear what is, and what isn’t, loyal behavior when it comes to proxy voting and shareholder engagement.” The proposal would remove two departmental inventions that are not consistent with ERISA and may be misused by fiduciaries with ulterior motives – the tiebreaker test and the participant preference provision. Under the tiebreaker test, a fiduciary can say that two investments are “equal” and then pick their preferred investment, which may include ESG funds. Similarly, fiduciaries can elicit the views of participants who support ESG investments and use that as a pretext to permit investments they otherwise would not be allowed to include under federal retirement laws. The proposed rule will be published in the Nov. 24 edition of the Federal Register, with public comments due 60 days after its publication.EBSA ensures the security of retirement, health, and other job-based benefits for American workers and their families. The agency is responsible for protecting more than 155 million workers, retirees, and their families, who are covered by approximately 2.8 million health plans, 837,000 private retirement plans, and 521,000 additional welfare benefit plans. Together, these plans hold about $15.2 trillion in assets.Employers and workers can contact EBSA at askebsa.dol.gov or call 866-444-3272 toll-free for help with private sector job-based retirement and health plans.Read the notice of proposed rulemaking on Loyalty and the Exclusive Purpose Rule in Selecting Plan Investments and Exercising Shareholder Rights.
